title: Pipes, Redirection and Searching Logs
oneLiner: Chain small commands together to answer real questions about a log file.
keyTakeaway: | sends one command's output into the next, > saves output to a file (replacing it), >> appends. grep finds lines, wc -l counts them, sort and uniq -c group them, awk picks out columns, head and tail trim. Together they answer most "what happened on this server?" questions in one line.
explanation:
Unix commands are deliberately small: each does one job on lines of text. The power comes from connecting them. A pipe, |, takes everything one command prints and feeds it to the next as input, so grep ERROR app.log | wc -l means "find the error lines, then count them".

Redirection sends output somewhere other than the screen. > file writes it into a file, replacing whatever was there -- easy to lose data with, so double-check. >> file adds to the end instead. 2> file captures error messages, which travel separately from normal output.

The toolkit you'll use most: grep (lines that match; -c counts, -i ignores case, -v inverts), head and tail (first or last lines; tail -f follows a log as it grows), wc -l (count lines), sort (sort lines; -n numerically, -r reversed), uniq -c (collapse repeated neighbouring lines into a count -- which is why you sort first), cut and awk (pull out columns: awk '{print $4}' prints the 4th space-separated field).

The log in this lesson is the kind of file you'd be handed during an incident. Each line is date, time, level, client IP, request and result. Questions like "how many errors?" and "who's hitting us hardest?" are a single pipeline each.
